$comment: Rate limiting rules — tasks/rate-limiting.md. Read at startup by src/config/rate-limit-rules.ts.
Every rule is `limit` requests per `windowMs` sliding window, counted in Redis so the limit holds
across instances. Going over returns 429 with Retry-After (typing frames are dropped instead —
there is no response to carry a header on).
Which buckets exist, and how each is keyed, is code — a key shape is a decision about what the
limit protects, and lives with the endpoint it guards. This file sets the numbers:
send    POST /api/messages                              per user, per conversation
search  GET  /api/search                                per user (a search spans conversations)
reads   GET  /api/messages, GET /api/conversations      per user
create  POST /api/conversations                         per user
typing  WebSocket `typing` frames                       per user, per conversation
Not metered, deliberately: GET /api/health, because the autoscaler polls it to find replicas;
GET /api/users, a fixed-size lookup with no caller-controlled cost, which is also what the scaling
probe samples request distribution with; and typing *stop* frames, so a throttled client can't
leave someone stuck as "typing" forever.
Precedence is env > this file > the defaults in src/config/rate-limit-rules.ts, so a deployment can
retune without a commit (RATE_LIMIT_MAX, SEARCH_RATE_LIMIT_MAX, READ_RATE_LIMIT_MAX,
CREATE_RATE_LIMIT_MAX, TYPING_RATE_LIMIT_MAX, and a _WINDOW_MS for each). RATE_LIMIT_CONFIG points
at a different file. A missing file is fine — the defaults are the shipped policy — but a malformed
or invalid one fails startup rather than quietly running numbers nobody chose.
On picking numbers: `send` is the one the task specifies. `search` is the tight one, because search
is the only endpoint whose cost grows with the caller's history. `reads` and `create` are runaway
script guards, not tight controls — set them low enough to stop a loop and high enough that nobody
honest ever meets them. Prefer a short window: it bounds a burst just as well and an exhausted
client recovers in seconds instead of being dark for a minute.
